analysis.one_liner: Caps hospital resident-physician work hours and protects whistleblowers who report violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have limited medical residents to 80-hour weeks with federal enforcement, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have used Medicare's rules for hospitals to limit medical residents—newly graduated doctors in training—to 24-hour shifts and 80-hour weeks, with at least one day off out of every seven. It would have required hospitals to tell residents their rights, let them complain anonymously to the government, fined hospitals up to $100,000 per training program for violations, and protected residents and other hospital workers who report violations from retaliation. To soften the cost, it appropriated federal money to pay hospitals' extra compliance expenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients treated by sleep-deprived doctors, since the bill cites research linking resident fatigue to medical errors—and the roughly $8 billion-a-year Medicare residency system the federal government already pays for. Medical residents themselves would gain enforceable work-hour limits and protection from being punished for reporting violations. Hospital employees who blow the whistle would get federal anti-retaliation protection.

how_it_helps.text: Limits residents to no more than 24 hours per shift, 80 hours per week, at least 10 hours between shifts, one day off in seven, one full weekend off per month, and no more than every-third-night hospital call [S3].

Cites research linking sleep deprivation in residency to higher rates of medical error, motor vehicle accidents, and depression, and an Institute of Medicine finding of up to 98,000 deaths a year from medical errors [S3].

Creates whistleblower protections for any hospital employee who in good faith reports working-hour violations to regulators, accreditation bodies, or management, and bans retaliation against them [S3].

Lets residents file complaints with HHS anonymously, requires annual anonymous compliance surveys made public by hospital and training program, and allows civil money penalties up to $100,000 per program per six months [S3].
Appropriates federal funds to reimburse hospitals for the reasonable incremental costs of complying, so the cost does not fall on hospital budgets or Medicare rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, hospitals would have faced new federal oversight, possible fines up to $100,000 per training program, and public disclosure of violations—though the bill appropriated money to cover their incremental compliance costs. Taxpayers would fund those compliance payments and enforcement. The medical education establishment would lose control over work-hour rules it had kept through self-regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Teaching hospitals and taxpayer-funded compliance payments

drawbacks.text: Handoffs of patients between doctors at shift changes carry their own risk; the bill acknowledges this by directing the Secretary to write rules ensuring quality of care during transfers, but any shift-limit system increases the number of handoffs [S3].

Hospitals could avoid penalties simply by submitting a corrective action plan, and the limits could be waived entirely during a declared emergency, raising questions about how strictly the rules would bite in practice [S3].
Open-ended appropriations to reimburse hospital compliance costs would add federal spending, and the limits could force hospitals to hire more staff at taxpayer expense [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—fewer errors from exhausted doctors treating patients—is backed by the research the bill itself cites, and the bill is thoughtfully designed: handoff rules, funded compliance costs, public disclosure, and whistleblower protection. The main costs are federal spending on hospital reimbursements and the inherent risks of more frequent patient handoffs. On balance the design is sound; the drawback is that it never got the chance to work.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine introduced the bill on April 30, 2003, with introductory remarks, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
It had only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and the Finance Committee took no further action—no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the record [S4].
The bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Teaching hospitals and the medical education establishment are better off: they kept self-regulation of resident work hours instead of facing enforceable federal limits, public disclosure of violations, and fines. Patients and residents gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on April 30, 2003.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action—no hearing, markup, or vote—leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Teaching hospitals and the medical education accreditor
against.role: Hospitals and the accreditation body governing residency programs
against.what_they_did: Resisted federal enforcement of resident work-hour limits in favor of industry self-regulation; shortly after similar bills were introduced, the accreditor adopted its own duty-hour rules, muddying the case for federal legislation.

sides.party_line_note: No floor votes ever occurred; the only record of support is one Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-run Finance Committee simply never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Teaching hospitals and medical residency programs
industries.note: The bill would have imposed enforceable work-hour limits, fines up to $100,000 per program, and public disclosure of violations—but it also appropriated federal money to pay hospitals' incremental compliance costs, so the financial hit was cushioned. Its interest ran against the public's here: hospitals' findings in the bill itself concede the medical community had not addressed fatigue-driven errors, and the industry preferred self-regulation to federal enforcement.

The federal government already pays about $8 billion a year to train residents through hospitals; the bill kept that arrangement but attached patient-safety strings to the money, so hospitals remained the permanent channel for publicly funded physician training [S3].
